paragraphs.text: You surely remember what happened to me when I was with you not long ago, after a long absence. Then the great mountain of unbelief, to use the language of the Gospel, was moved to faith, when the most wise Eusebius made a decision in his old age worthy of his grey hairs, if indeed one ought to consider this

a human decision at all, and not rather some divine help from the One who governs human affairs for good. At that time I was astonished at how unexpected the wonder was: how such a man, formerly in unbelief, had exceeded the measure of his unbelief many times over by the greatness of his faith. Then, as our conversation went on, talk turned [?] to the questions raised about fate, and you, my honoured and sacred head, asked me to write you a letter describing the debate on this subject that I had held with one of the philosophers in the great city of Constantine. So, having found a little leisure, I have cut the account down to a few words, as far as possible, and I set it out for you in a simple and unadorned narrative. I have taken particular care that it should not run far beyond the bounds of a letter by stretching to the length of a treatise.

I was putting forward some arguments for our religion to a man educated in secular learning, as far as one could guess from what he said, and I was trying to persuade him to leave Hellenism and assent to our doctrine. But he went to great lengths to argue that choosing what we decide is not within the power of those who wish to choose. Instead he made human life depend on a kind of necessity, without which none of the things that happen in us could happen. With this argument he deflected mine: if it was fated for him to become a Christian, he would certainly become one even if we did not wish it; but if the necessity of fate prevented it, he could not become one, since no device could be found that would overpower fate. When he said this, I naturally thought that he was avoiding learning anything about the faith because he was deeply set in Hellenism, and that he was deflecting the course of my argument in this way. But he did not give up. He persisted in the same claims, saying that all things are yoked under the necessity of fate, that fate presides over all that exists, and that everything bows to its turning: the length of life, differences of character, choices of how to live, the constitution of bodies and inequalities of rank. So the one who comes to rule by fate certainly rules, another is a slave for the same reason, and likewise one is rich and another poor. Health and sickness of body, an early death and a long life, have the same cause too. The man who shares in life for only a short time and the man who stretches his life over a long time each end up as they are, not by their own impulse but from that necessity. Natural death and forced death are allotted by nothing other than fate, and so are the many different kinds of violent death, whether they come by accident, by hanging, by a judge's sentence, or even by a plot. He also made that same cause responsible for the still more general and widespread calamities: earthquakes and shipwrecks, floods and disasters by fire, and all such kinds of evil. And he added that in the pursuits of life the reasoning of the one choosing is never in control. Rather, all men, in subjection to the power of fate,

serve it, whether they are philosophers or orators, farmers or sailors, whether they live in marriage or choose the unmarried life. He insisted that the same necessity governs both virtue and vice. So, by this inviolable allotment, one man devotes himself to the higher life, living without possessions and free, while another robs tombs, turns pirate, lives a dissolute life, or is made effeminate in the life of a prostitute. Going through all such things, he thought he had shown a strong reason for not accepting our teaching: it is not in our power to choose freely whatever we wish. Instead one must wait for that necessity. If it gives the signal for such a movement, one must accept the teaching of necessity, even unwillingly; but without it, however much one chooses it, it cannot happen.

While he was going through these and similar things, I asked him whether he thought that what is called by the name of fate is some God who holds power over all things, by whose will, he believed, each particular thing is ordered. But he condemned the great foolishness of my question and said: "You seem to me to have understood nothing of heavenly things. Otherwise you would have known the power of fate, and how the power of things that happen inviolably in sequence has been grasped." This statement also seemed strange to me, and I asked to learn something clearer: did he imagine fate to be some power of choice, absolute and without a master, seen as holding a supreme authority, or did he take it to be something else? He took up the same argument again and said: "Consider the man who has studied the motion of the heavenly bodies: the circle of the zodiac, and the twelve segments in it, set at equal distances from one another and marked out by the outlines of the signs seen in it. He has understood the power of each of the stars: what strength each has by nature on its own, and what their conjunction produces from their particular blending with one another, as the property of each one's power is mingled when it approaches another and separated again when it moves away. He knows what the passing beneath of the lower star brings about, what the eclipse of the higher one brings about as it is passed, and what its restoration brings about. He knows the varied configurations of stars as they come together and move apart, traced out in triangles or scalene figures or forming some other of the figures studied in geometry. The man who has understood these and similar things will know what fate means: what is brought about by necessity, through an inviolable sequence, according to a particular interweaving of the stars, is expressed by the name of fate."

This too seemed strange to me, for I understood nothing of what he said, since I had not been educated in that learning. So I asked him to make his meaning clear to me by means through which I could grasp the idea of fate. For I said that the starry circles are set one within another, that within it they revolve with a motion contrary to the rotation of the fixed sphere, and that all of them turn within the circle of the zodiac:

these things, I said, I had heard from others as well. Nor did I doubt what follows from them. The rays of the luminaries approach and withdraw according to the revolution proper to each sphere. The lower star passes beneath, and the higher one is hidden from our sight if it comes behind the one passing beneath. I accepted everything that may reasonably be inferred from this: whether some figure is formed by these motions when a circle, by its own movement, carries round the star set on it, so that the star comes directly in line with the one above or slants aside as it passes; and whether the period of each of these takes a short interval of time or a longer one, depending on the relative size of each circle, so that the return necessarily moves faster or slower. All these and similar matters I asked him to pass over in silence, and simply to disclose the power of fate to me clearly. Is that which is understood by the name of fate some God, holding power over everything and governing all things as he pleases by the superiority of his power? Or does he suppose that the power of fate serves some other, higher activity, so that in a way fate itself lies under another fate and is disposed together with the superior cause? If it is believed to have power over all things, the logic of the argument allows us to conclude [?] that it is subject to nothing. But if he insists that fate follows the motion of the stars and yet rules all things by some violent necessity, it would be safer to ascribe this all-powerful authority to what leads rather than to what follows. In that case he should call the stars the causes of these things, or the revolution of the fixed sphere, or the circles seen within it, or the circle drawn obliquely across the heavens. For suppose these did not move, and did not come together or apart through their everlasting revolution, but always stayed the same in the same configuration: then fate would not exist. If, then, the motion of the stars gives birth to fate, it is wrong to think that fate rules over everything else. It is a slave to the higher cause, and it would not exist if there were no motion.

"But that is not so," said the philosopher. "Our teaching does not hold that fate exists by itself as a distinct reality. Rather, there is one sympathy among all beings. The universe is continuous with itself, and the individual things within the whole are held together in one common breath, as in a single body, all the parts inclining toward one another. For this reason, since the upper region has the leading role, all earthly things are disposed together with what leads and incline toward it in accordance with the motion above, and things here are necessarily moved along with it. Each of the stars, as has been said, is seen to have a different power. In medical pharmacy, the qualities of the ingredients, mixed skilfully in a certain proportion, produce from their common blend something different from what each was before they were mixed. In the same way the stellar powers have different properties, and the varied interweaving of these properties, as the stars approach and separate, produces the varied

differences in the way lives turn out, as though an emanation reached us unbroken from there. This is also why the predictions of future events made by those who study such matters with special care do not miss. Suppose a hot or narcotic drug is blended with a salty or astringent one: the medical expert foretells the property that will arise from mixing substances of different natures, what it will do, how long its strength will last, and for whom it will be deadly and for whom a remedy. In the same way, the man who has carefully attended to the things above and understood the nature of each of them will know what the power arising from their particular interweaving will bring about. Yet this emanation does not stay the same even for a short time. Because the motion of the stars woven together is never at rest, the emanation too is necessarily altered along with the continual change of motion. It is always being remixed with the variety of the motion, and its activities change together with the movement of the stars. Each person brought into life draws whatever portion of it falls to him in that instant of time, and becomes what the property of that part foretold and brought about. For just as, necessarily, the shape of the engraving is stamped on wax pressed into the mould of a seal, so a man's life is stamped according to the property of whatever particle of the power flowing from the stars' motion it meets. It becomes what that portion of the emanation, drawn at the very beginning of life, held within itself. Once a man has been stamped [?] according to the power seen there, he is necessarily shaped in the character of his life, doing or suffering the things whose beginnings or causes were laid down by that first encounter with the stellar emanation."

When he said this, I answered him: "Will you not stop going through these trifles and this nonsense with me? You make that indivisible part, shared for an instant, which you say flows into us from above, the cause of everything in us. Yet you do not say whether it is alive and capable of choice. Nor can you show how something lifeless and without substance, with no impulse of its own by nature, prevails over living beings. Over all deliberation and the foresight that comes from reasoning, over education and diligence and the pursuits of virtue, your argument sets up, like a tyrant or a master, something lifeless and without choice, unstable and fleeting, indivisible and without substance. You make the existence and governance of all beings depend on its power. Do you not see what absurdities your argument is carried into? If that portion of the emanation has such power that it shapes, according to itself, those born at its first passing, then surely it will govern the existence of beings not as following but as leading. Therefore it will bring forth the one being born according to its own power, and it will not be serving the mere chance of the child's birth. But here it is unclear which of the two leads the other, since both coincide equally in that instant. For the man, even before he leaves the womb,

[?] follows human birth. For the one is always in motion, but the other is not always being born. One moves in its own sequence, and the other again proceeds on its own, independently, and no necessity binds together things that are separate by nature. But if your argument maintains that the cause of everything in life lies in that portion of time, consider how many myriads of masters and tyrants every day and every night produce through those fine, instantaneous divisions of time. Day and night are divided, as you say, into twenty-four hours. Each hour is split into sixty parts, and each of these parts is cut up again into the same number. And, as those of you who probe more finely into such observations say, each of these parts is refined yet again by a division into the same number. So the multitude gathered from these of those instantaneous gods, or masters, or tyrants, or whatever one should call them, comes to more than twenty-one myriads. And if one hour produces so many myriads of portions for us, then the twenty-four hours, each multiplied in the same way, give birth to countless myriads of portions. Yet your teaching insists that each of these has an inviolable power. It follows that none of them is idle. You would not say that inactivity belongs to power: power is surely seen in its activity. So the effects of these powers are equal too, and there will necessarily be as many human births every hour as there are parts. And if power must be ascribed equally to each portion, the equality of their power will make all men equally kings, long-lived, powerful, well endowed and happy, and everything else that is thought to belong to the more honoured lot. For lacking any of these amounts to an accusation that the power is deficient. No one would ascribe equal power to one who has accomplished great things and one who has accomplished small ones. For example, one man has passed a hundred years in a rich and happy old age, flourishing in his children, attended by his grandchildren, rejoicing in the generation after them, free from disease and

harm, held in honour, free from grief, abundantly wealthy, and blessed in everything counted precious in this life. Another man was strangled as soon as he was brought into the light, like many infants born to prostitutes or from adultery, whom the mothers who conceived them unlawfully put to death with their own hands, hiding the proof of their guilt by death. Where is the power of the portion in these cases? Why was the strength of fate not enough for the same length of life? If your teaching thinks it must ascribe power to fate, its strength will be shown equally in all beings. It will not prevail in one case and be powerless in another, if it truly is understood as power; and power is known by its effects. So life will have no inequality, and all men alike will show in themselves the highest measure of happiness, since by your account all lie under fate, and you say it can always do everything. If, then, this fate can do everything and always, it will be able to do everything in every case. Yet there are many different conditions of life among men, in rank and wealth, in length of years, in bodily constitution, and in everything for which someone is called blessed or wretched. So the inequality of the results clearly shows that the portion or fate your argument has invented cannot do everything. If we consider long life a work of power, an early death is surely a sign of weakness. So we must hold that among the fated portions one is weak and another powerful. For since a short life is the opposite of a long one, each of these surely comes about through opposite causes. No one would attach blessedness and wretchedness to the same cause; if the one is achieved through power, the other surely came about through a lack of power. For wretchedness consists in nothing other than being unable to become blessed. Yet the wretched are the majority in this life. So fate is shown to have more weakness than power. Where, then, is that invincible, all-powerful and inviolable necessity in which authority over everything arranged in life is supposed to rest, when the logic of the argument has proved it weak in most cases?

"But," you will say, "fate wills this for one man and does not will the same for another; it can do in both cases what it wills." Then you must certainly also give the cause of this difference in its choices. This man and that man are both human. You see no difference of nature between the two, and neither has good or evil by his own choice. But this one, a little ahead in time, sprang from his mother's womb, because nature happened to deliver him then; the other came after him, either immediately or shortly afterwards. And from then on the same life is not allotted to both. One is happy, or a king if it so happens, wrapped in gold and purple at his very birth. The other, the child of some poor man or slave, is not swaddled by his parents even in rags. What wrong did he do by coming a little earlier or later in time, not by his own purpose but by the motion of nature, that for this very reason he should be allotted a life of dishonour? What kind of … of the mistress [?]

…what defense will you find for that fate of yours in such matters? Where is justice? Where is piety? Where is holiness? Or do you say that fate cares for none of these things, that it does not look to virtue and takes no care for anything good? Then if these things are not its concern, it will surely busy itself with their opposite, for estrangement from the good plainly shows an affinity with evil. But perhaps you say that neither the one nor the other is its concern? Then you are saying that it is soulless and without choice, with no perception of better or worse. But if it has neither soul nor choice, and is not seen to have any subsistence of its own, how can you claim that it has so much power that it rules over creatures endowed with choice? How can the non-subsistent master what subsists, what has no share in life master what shares in life, the soulless master the ensouled, the choiceless master those who live by choice, what is incapable of virtue master those who pursue virtue, and in a word the non-existent master the existent? In what, then, does the subsistence of this much-bandied name consist? It is not a living being; it is not seen within any bounds; it is not thought to be God. For how could that be God which does not look to virtue and justice? And what is none of these things, what is it? But it seems that what you call fate is the ever-present moment of time, for time extends alongside every motion, whether of rivers, of stars, or of men. And it makes no difference whether one sits by the water and marks off the tiny segments of ever-present time by the motion of the current, or by a ship carried along by the wind, or by men walking, or by stars moving. For in everything that moves from place to place there is one definition of motion: a shift from where it is to where it is not. If, then, neither the flow of streams nor the movement of ships nor the travel of men, though they mark the intervals of time, produce fates, how do you mold the temporal points of the stars' motion into a source of fate, and say that this hour, or some tiny fraction of the hour marked at this point in the stars' motion, becomes fate? Why then do human births not coincide with every single point? For I shall take up the same argument again. Whatever is the cause of a man's faring well or badly must surely also be the cause of his existing at all. If, then, what comes after birth is due to those things, birth too must be due to the same things; but if birth is not in their power, neither is what follows it. And that birth is not in their power is clear from this: human births do not flow without a break, like a river, along with the continuous passing stream of time; births come at intervals. But in the generation of those fates which flowing time produces through the ceaseless course of the stars there is no interval whatever, whether grasped by sense or by thought. What that fate is, then, whether it is one more general fate or many fates finely divided along with the segments of time, our reasoning has not yet been able to grasp

by any consistent line of thought. You say the stars move? We too set against this the motion of rivers. But the stars move continually? So do the rivers, throughout. But the stars move in time? Neither are the rivers outside time. But no temporal beginning can be found for the stars' motion? And what beginning in time will you conceive for the rivers? But the stars always move in the same way and manner? Nor would anyone ascribe a contrary motion to the rivers, since water by nature always flows down from higher ground to the slope below. So either grant that the motion of rivers too begets fates of some kind, or we shall not concede this power to the motion of the stars either. "But," he says, "the Ram or the Bull has this power, and each of the planets that power. So whenever one of the planets, carried round periodically by the circle, comes into one of these signs, either alone or with others, the conjunction of powers produces such-and-such a life for the one who happens to be born at that hour." What empty talk! You say the Bull, as it happens, is servile, because this animal is broken under the yoke, and the Ram beneficent because of the bearing of young; and that a planet, coming into one of these signs or into one of those revolving in the opposite direction, fashions such-and-such a lot for those being born, by the power naturally inherent in it, through the mingling of properties. What then? Tell me: is the bull a beast of burden willingly? Do you say the ram is glad to be shorn? And is the harmful and numbing power in the one that circles the highest pole, or the heat in the fiery one, or the power in any other of the observed bodies, present in them willingly or unwillingly? If they are in evil willingly and become harmful by choice, whoever says so plainly condemns them to misfortune, because, though the better lot lay within their power, they took pleasure in the baser. But if each of them is what you suppose not by choice but has become so from some necessity, then again some other fate, set above them, spun out the particular properties of their natures and powers. So one must necessarily look for other stars higher than these, with a motion peculiar to themselves, whose particular combination, by some necessity of fate, made the Bull servile, or the Ram harmful, or the Crab headless, or whatever else the nonsense of the wise recounts about each of them. And if these things that appear to us are what they are by the necessity of some fate, reason will surely have to conceive, for that higher necessity as well, another compelling cause of its condition, and for that one another, and yet another for the other; and so the argument, running on to infinity, will never come to a stop, fabricating fate upon fate, lot upon lot, and necessity upon necessity. As I was going through these points and by such reasoning driving the argument into absurdity, the philosopher I was debating with leaned forward and broke in as the argument was rushing on. "Why do you fight against plain fact?" he said. "Why do you not follow those who have discerned the truth of all things by means of numbers? If the hour of a child's birth is taken precisely, they predict in order the whole life of the one born: the length of time, the manner of life, the peculiarities of character, dangerous situations, marriages and children and the winning of honors, or on the contrary childlessness and diseases and disgrace and a short life and the miseries of poverty. When these things have been foretold precisely and the outcome has borne witness to the truth, what argument have you left for disbelieving

in the necessity of fate?" I said I would look into the causes of such predictions a little later, and asked whether the cause of such outcomes was irrational and accidental, or whether they also discovered some rational account along with this observation, so that what happens does not happen against all likelihood. "Very much so," he said; "there is indeed a rational account of what happens. For when, from a particular coincidence of the qualities in the stars, a certain bodily temperament is formed in the one being born, the man who has precisely mastered the study of the heavens foresees both that this temperament will be formed in the child and that his life can last up to such-and-such a measure: longer if the bodily temperament is more robust, and shorter again if it is more sickly." I laughed at what he had said and told him, "You have been holding without our noticing that fates are the offspring of Galen and Hippocrates and their like! For they too, dismissing the motion of the stars, predict the future by conjecture from what lies before them: when hollow eyes, sunken temples, and a forehead with the skin dried tight forebode death. But in many cases," I said, "where people's bodies were in a sickly state and they were all but expected to die, medicine has unspun the threads of such a fate in the opposite direction. So Plato's account tells of Herodicus the trainer, that through his skill in gymnastics he could not restore his body to full health, since his disease was fatal; but by always ingeniously putting off the death that was at hand, he secured for himself not safety of life but a prolonging of death. And so he lasted even into old age, contriving by a long death not to die. So not even by this argument is your fate found to be unbreakable, if some art is found that loosens its necessity." "But," he said, "such an argument does nothing to undo the proof of fate drawn from predictions. For this too could be foretold by one who has precisely examined the motion of the heavens, so that for one person death is foretold as certain and for another as doubtful." And I said, "That is not how the argument for necessity holds good. The account of the contingent, which may turn out either way, is one thing; the account of the unchangeable is another, and it cannot be found among contingent things: it must be this altogether, or else the other. To have one's hopes wavering between both outcomes is far from the reasoning of necessity. But I put this to him: where does he think the prediction of future events gets its credibility?" He said, "You have often heard me explain it, and still you ask about the same things: that the stars have certain particular powers, and the ceaseless motion of their course, through their particular combinations, produces countless differences of power. So whoever is brought into life by birth is stamped with the portion of time that fell to him, as shaped in this way by the stars; and whatever that hour's power is found to contain,

that he will necessarily have in his life as well, and not otherwise." "What then," I said, "of the disasters of war, earthquakes, the collapse of cities, the wrecks of great merchant ships lost with all hands, floods, conflagrations, chasms, and every other such form of total destruction? How will these keep the account of prediction intact? How many calamities has life displayed in former times, and how many in our own? The flood in the time of Noah, and the burning of Sodom? Or the Egyptian army sunk beneath the Red Sea? Or the later slaughters of the foreign nations, those countless killings? Or the sudden death, in a short time, of the Israelite people, struck down in many tens of thousands? Or the one hundred and eighty-five thousand Assyrians killed in a single moment of time, and the histories of the evils that followed, in the Median and Greek disasters, in great battles at sea and on land, and all such things, whose memory becomes a teacher to those who come after? Even if we pass over all these, what has been recorded in our own lifetime would be enough to bear witness to what I am saying. Who does not know the great metropolis of Bithynia, counted among the most eminent of cities? Who is unaware of broad and spacious Thrace, and how war utterly destroyed the one, and an earthquake with fire the other, in an instant? How many children were there, how many infants? Those in middle life, the aged, free and slave, rulers and subjects, rich and poor, healthy and sick, all perished in a single moment. The fire devoured them all alike; for all of them their houses became tombs. Where are those intertwinings of the stars that determine for men the differences of their lives? Did a single conjunction of the stars bring all of them to birth, and did the Crab, standing in the horoscope, impose the same lot on them all? Yet the countless differences of age and rank bear witness that they were not all born at the same time as one another. If, then, the time of birth was different for each, while the sameness of their disasters admitted no variation arising from the cause connected with birth, then by this too the doctrine of prediction is shown to be incoherent and unfounded." "But," he says, "there is a fate of a ship, and of a city, and of a whole nation, which spins out what follows according to its first founding; and the things contained are of necessity affected along with what contains them." What, then, is the Eileithyia of shipbuilding? What is the birth of a city? From what beginning do we observe the birth of a nation? The woodcutter fells the timber; the timber merchant trades in it; the shipbuilder buys the material with money and divides the craft among the work. One man saws the wood into planks; another builds the keel; another is busy fitting the undergirding cables; one finished off the prow, and another the stern. One man sees to the mast, another to the yard; some twist the flax into ropes; others take care of the rudder-shafts for the helmsman; others make the decks and the sailcloth; others add the ornament of painting. Others again smear the joints with pitch and construct the bilge in the middle. Surely they do not all do their own parts at the same time: one works now, others a little later; for one the task has already been finished,

while another is still seen at work. When, then, will the wise set fate over the ship? When the wood is bought, or when it is cut, or when it is worked, or when iron is applied to it, or when it is fastened with bolts? Since the tasks of shipbuilding are many and various and are not carried out at the same time as one another, what moment will he assign to fate, so that the ship, receiving the necessity of sinking, destroys along with itself those who sail in it? And what would you say about cities? When do they think fate takes control of a city? When those eager to found it first conceive a plan of settlement? When they reckon up the advantages of the site, or when they mark out its plan, or when they actually set iron to the work, or lay the stones, or gather the materials? Which of these is the beginning of its founding? And what would you say about the nation that was wiped out by the disasters of war? What lot, taking its beginning against them from where, slaughtered some and reduced others to slavery through captivity? How did Hannibal or Caesar, or Alexander of Macedon, among whatever peoples they campaigned, bring about an equal fate for all, so overpowering that necessity that all were brought together into the same measure of evil? Moreover, one can see from what follows that it is unreasonable to suppose that the fates of cities produce the stellar configurations at work in the collapses caused by earthquakes. Who does not know that such afflictions of the earth occur not only in inhabited places but also in uninhabited ones? If anyone has come to know the mountain of the Sangagi, which lies near the borders of the Bithynians, by his own experience, or has heard of it by report, he will find the truth of what I say: at the very passes of the road the whole ridge has sunk down and become a fearful sight to travelers. Such afflictions occur also in the lands of the Paphlagonians. In some places human dwellings have been dragged down along with these chasms, but in many places the ground affected by such an event is shown to be bare of inhabitants. And why must I go through the Cypriots, the Pisidians, and the Achaeans one by one, among whom there are many proofs of what I say? But the reason we have mentioned these things is that all such events are afflictions of the earth. If, then, human habitation happens to be found in the place, those people too, by every necessity, share in the misfortune of the place; but if it is free of inhabitants, the misfortune of the place has brought no harm to human beings. What, then, is the necessity of fate, when inhabited and uninhabited places alike undergo such an affliction? For if they could show that the earth was formed part by part and not all at once, their empty talk might perhaps have had an opening: that when this part of the earth was being founded, and this combination of stars was matched to it, this or that came about by necessity. But since all things are understood to have come into being together, heaven, earth, and sea, and according to the account of Moses the earth even precedes the making and the motion of the stars, how

will they attribute the cause of particular events on earth to the motion of the stars? If, then, the earth is coeval with the stars and draws from them no cause either of collapse or of endurance, and if such afflictions occur within particular bounded places, then it is not the necessity of fate but some other particular cause that operates in such events. When, therefore, the earth suffers something of this kind and brings about such disasters, its inhabitants shaken down along with the collapse, what will they say who worship fate and lay it down that the motion of the stars presides over all that exists? How do things stand there with the infant, the babe, the youth, the man, the father, the old man, the well-born, the patrician, the hired laborer, the prisoner? Neither the time of their birth nor any difference of rank keeps them from an equal share in the evils. Further, who does not know that the very extreme of all defilement is intercourse with daughters, marriage with sisters, and lawlessness toward mothers? If this came about by some necessity of lot, it would surely have been dared in our regions too; but since such defilement is dared only by the Persian nation and by those who have been taught their customs, it follows clearly that each person's choice becomes his lot and fate, choosing by its own authority what seems good to it. Further, they may say that according to the particular inclinations of different regions certain particular motions of the stars are found, and that this is why some marry their mothers while others kill strangers and eat human flesh, the position of the stars bearing peculiarly upon them. Such an argument belongs to people altogether uneducated and unversed in the study of reality, who think that the lot from above is imprinted on people according to particular regions of the earth; for in that case earthly things would be found to have more authority than heavenly ones, if the heavenly were thought to be ordered according to the earthly. Nevertheless, so that they cannot say even this, we shall add the following to refute their deluded supposition. The Jewish race has spread over nearly every part of the earth: eastern, southern, inland, western, and northern peoples, nearly every nation, are mingled with Jews living among them. How is it, then, that no necessity of the stars in any of these places has had the power to grant any member of that nation exemption from mutilation? Rather, amid the countless combinations of the stars, however the newborn child happens to come into the world, it is always in the same condition, its nature undergoing the mutilation at the appointed cycle of days. He said, "We have not yet examined by what reason the things governed by laws among many nations escape the necessity of the stars. But the prediction of future events would be thought no small proof that what has been allotted to each person is inviolable. For how was it that so-and-so, having learned in advance that he would live this number of years and meet with such-and-such events in his life, was not deceived, unless some necessity had inviolably spun out that these things must happen to him, and had made them plain to the one predicting them through his particular observation of the signs marked out by number?" I said that in such matters it was better to seem ignorant than to give occasion for laughter to those who know little of our doctrines; but nevertheless, with a little thought…

[?] ...of those who make a mockery of our teaching, I will set out the whole explanation of this matter in a few words, as best I can. There is a certain power that is by nature hostile to the human race, and it is known from things contrary to the good nature. Countless proofs of this could be drawn from plain facts, but I do not think it necessary at present to go through, in order, everything that has led people to believe this is so. The divine nature is seen in every good idea and every good name. From it come life, light, truth, justice, wisdom, incorruption and every good thing the mind can grasp: it is all of these, and it bestows all of these. The power known from the opposites, then, is recognized in everything that is seen as the opposite of each of these goods. So among human beings it brings death instead of life, deception instead of truth, and for each better thing the evil set against it. For whatever by nature leads to the ruin of human beings is dear to it. Poisoners often sweeten the deadly drug with honey. They do not do this to please their victim's taste, but to hide from him what is destroying him. In the same way this destructive nature, whose aim is to turn human beings away from the good nature, takes on the outward forms of certain good things. It covers the hidden design of its deceit with predictions and cures, so that the wretched human race may pay attention to these, think them good, and have no desire for what is truly good by nature. That is why, whatever kind of foreknowledge someone has been taken in by through some deception, the deceptive power of the demons answers him in that same way: in the inspection of livers and in augury, in omens, in necromancy, in casting nativities. Each of these foretells what is to come, though not in the same way but in different ways. Now the man who points to the future by means of a liver, the man who guesses what will be from some omen, and the man who watches the flight of a bird do not claim to foretell such things by the necessity of fate. In the same way there is one cause, as has been said, behind this kind of prediction: I mean the deceptive working of the demons. So if one of these predictions has at some time come true by chance (if indeed it ever came true at all), that does not prove the power of fate. Otherwise every kind of prediction could just as reasonably be made out to draw its force from fate. Then we would have one fate that is the dream, another that is the observation of twitchings, and another made up of augury, or omens, or some other signs. But if nothing prevents those cases from involving prediction without involving fate, then neither, if some prediction the casters of nativities made from their numbers has come true, would that be enough ground for belief, since such things do not easily come true [?]. Moreover, the forecasts of those who profess such arts are neither precise nor unambiguous,

but they prepare many ways of escape for themselves about the outcome, in case what they said is proved wrong. They also work out excuses in advance for those who care about such things, so that the failure is blamed not on an error in their science but on the recording of the hour. As a rule their predictions are oblique and hedge between two possible outcomes, so that whatever happens may seem to have been foretold. For often a man who has studied the hour of someone's birth has announced that he will be famous and stand above others. Then, when that person met with extraordinary disasters, the man insisted that his prediction had not been wrong at all, since the person had a greater share of evils than others. The history of our own time bears witness to this. When the emperor Valens ruled over the Romans, a deception of this kind drove a certain man to rebel against his rule. He set out with the prediction of the casters of nativities as fuel for his daring. But his attempt ended in such a way that the very man who had been marked out for the highest offices became all the more famous for the magnitude of his disaster. Most people took this as confirmation of astrology: a magnitude of disaster had befallen the man in place of a magnitude of good things. For my part, I do not yet treat the fact that predictions about these things go astray as strong proof that the doctrine of fate does not stand. My reason is rather that the deceptive power of the demons contrives its predictions by many other devices as well. For there was also a certain prophetic water that brought derangement and madness on those who tasted it. There was also a vapor rising from below through an opening, and if it entered a woman's inward parts, it made her belly swell and produced ecstasy of mind and derangement from her settled state. All these things seemed divine and prophetic to the deceived. Yet among those who guess the future from signs in livers or fire, or who watch the flights of birds, no one has attributed the power of prediction to fate. Rather, they put such things down to some demonic possession. So I say this: either there is no foretelling at all, since predictions are refuted by many contradictions; or, if someone shows that it does foretell some future events, then what we understand in the case of each of the other things achieved by prediction must also be held true of this kind of prediction. For the same holds in all these cases: they miss the mark most of the time, and in some cases the prediction seems not to stray from the truth of what will happen. In the same way the deceptive nature of the demons achieves its aim through this and through every other device. For the demons' chief concern, above all else, is to turn human beings away from looking to God and so from securing for themselves their share of good things. The easily deceived are convinced that the affairs of life depend not on the divine will but on a particular interweaving of the stars and on the power that flows from it, and this conviction serves the aim of the harmful nature of the demons more than anything else. If, then, it pleases the demons to turn human beings away from God, and error about these things does turn them away, then this error is clearly shown to be a demonic working. Through deception it leads astray those who think that all power lies in these things and do not look to the almighty authority of God.
